content: There are no specific diagnostic laboratory findings that are definitively associated with sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). However, certain laboratory abnormalities may be observed in some cases. Some infants with SIDS may present with anemia. If anemia is suspected, it is recommended to perform a complete blood count (CBC) to evaluate the condition. In cases where infection is suspected, a range of laboratory tests should be considered to assess potential underlying causes. These include: Blood gas analysis (BGA) to evaluate respiratory or metabolic abnormalities. Blood lactate levels to assess for lactic acidosis. Blood glucose levels to evaluate for hypoglycemia. Liver enzyme tests to assess hepatic function. Lumbar puncture (LP) to obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for analysis. Serum electrolyte levels to detect imbalances. Blood urea levels to evaluate renal function. Calcium and phosphate levels to assess for metabolic disturbances. Urinalysis and urine culture to identify potential urinary tract infections. Virology screening to detect viral infections. Bacterial screening to identify bacterial pathogens. Maternal biomarkers may also provide insight into the risk of SIDS. Elevated levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) during pregnancy have been associated with congenital anomalies such as neural tube defects, omphalocele, gastroschisis, and fetal bowel obstructions. These congenital conditions are known to increase the risk of SIDS.
